analysis.one_liner: Requires brokers to disclose their pay for selling mutual funds and tightens fund board independence.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2003 with one Republican and two Democratic cosponsors, the bill went no further than the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required brokers to tell fund buyers, in writing, how much they are paid to sell a mutual fund. It also would have forced brokerage commissions into the published expense ratios investors see, shrunk the share of fund directors who have financial ties to the fund company, banned conflicted directors from chairing fund boards, and required disclosure of portfolio manager pay. Three SEC and GAO studies would have examined fund oversight, investor literacy, and fund advertising.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday investors who buy mutual funds, especially retirement savers whose 401(k) and IRA money sits in them. They would see, at the moment of purchase, exactly how much their broker earns from the sale, and fund expense ratios would include brokerage commissions that are currently buried, making it easier to comparison-shop and press for lower fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirement savers and mutual fund investors

how_it_helps.text: Brokers would have to disclose in writing, by the time a fund purchase completes, the amount of any compensation they receive from any source in connection with the sale, and the disclosure could not be buried solely in a prospectus or SEC filing.

Brokerage commissions paid by a fund, as a dollar amount and percentage of assets, would have to be included in fee and expense disclosures, including expense-ratio calculations, so investors could see the full cost of owning the fund.

Fund boards would have to be at least 75 percent independent, up from the old minimum of 40 percent outside directors; no board action could depend on the vote of a conflicted director; and an independent committee of outside directors would pick board nominees and set their qualifications.

Interested directors would need shareholder re-approval at least every five years and annual findings that they have no material business or family ties to the fund or its major service providers, and the definition of an interested person would be broadened to cover people with recent ties to the fund's adviser or service providers.

The bill would have directed the SEC to study whether an independent Mutual Fund Oversight Board with inspection and enforcement power should be created, required disclosure of portfolio managers' pay structures and their stakes in the fund, and commissioned studies on investor financial literacy and on misleading fund advertising.

analysis.who_pays: Mutual fund companies, their investment advisers, and brokers selling funds. Brokers would have to reveal commissions that many customers never see; fund companies would have to replace conflicted directors, including industry-tied chairs, with independents; and advisers would have to disclose how they pay their portfolio managers. Compliance costs and fee pressure would fall on the industry, and any of it passed through would ultimately touch investors.

drawbacks.text: The requirements are paperwork-heavy: written broker disclosures, annual independence findings, expanded director definitions, and four separate SEC and GAO studies would add compliance costs, some of which fund companies could pass along to investors in higher expenses.

Disclosure tells investors what a broker earns but does not cap it or ban revenue-sharing, so a fund with high fees and high broker pay remains legal; the bill relies on transparency to push costs down rather than mandating lower ones.

Tightening board independence could shrink the pool of directors with deep industry experience, and critics of governance rules argue that independent directors may not in practice negotiate lower fees for shareholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For savers, the potential gain is real: fund fees and hidden broker payments are a chronic drag on retirement returns, and knowing what a broker collects at the point of sale is information investors cannot otherwise get. The costs are modest by comparison — mostly compliance paperwork and study expenses — though the bill's weakness is that it informs rather than forbids, leaving high-fee arrangements intact so long as they are disclosed. The stronger provisions, like a 75 percent independent board and a ban on conflicted chairs, target the structural conflict that lets fund companies set their own fees.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in November 2003, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Daniel Akaka introduced the bill on November 5, 2003, joined by Senator Peter Fitzgerald, a Republican, and Senator Joseph Lieberman.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced; that was the last action it ever received.
The bill sat in committee with no hearing, markup, or floor vote recorded through the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005, so none of its provisions became law.

The bill's provisions covered broker compensation disclosure, inclusion of brokerage commissions in expense ratios, fund board independence requirements, portfolio manager compensation disclosure, and studies of fund oversight, investor literacy, and fund advertising.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mutual fund companies, advisers, and brokers kept collecting fees and sales commissions with no new disclosure requirements, while investors gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — one Republican and two Democratic cosponsors — but died without a roll call, so no party split on it was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have forced at least 75 percent independent boards, barred conflicted directors from chairing and from decisive votes, and required re-election of interested directors every five years, weakening the fund industry's control over the boards that approve its fees. Investors would gain lower-fee pressure; the industry would lose control.

Brokers would have to disclose in writing, at the time of sale, how much they earn from selling a fund, exposing payments many customers never see. Transparency at the point of sale would make it harder to steer customers into funds that pay the broker more.

The bill would require funds to disclose how portfolio managers are paid and their stakes in the fund, and to count the adviser's service providers among the people who count as conflicted directors. More visibility into how the people running the fund are compensated.
